item.content:encoded: A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday. The helicopter crashed due to a technical malfunction in an area under the jurisdiction of the Saudi National Guard Ministry, the statement added. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis released footage later on Sunday of what they said was a Saudi AH-6i helicopter being shot down by a missile while carrying out what they described as hostile activities near Najran. The footage did not clearly show the incident, and Reuters could not immediately verify the Houthis' claim. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities. On Saturday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X that the group had shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter near Najran. It was not clear if that referred to the same incident. Al-Maliki commented on Saree's post on Sunday with a photo of several Apaches lined up, saying: "You claim to have shot it down, but it will enter the battlefield soon." Separately, the Saudi civil defence said on Sunday that six people were injured after a projectile it said was fired by Houthis fell on a residential area in Najran. Najran has been hit by attacks from the Houthis in recent weeks as fighting between the coalition and the Yemen-based group escalated, with the [USN:L1N4620VJ TEXT:"Yemen conflict"] becoming another front in the US-led war with Iran .

item.title: Deaths confirmed after 'serious incident,' fire at Canada military base in Alberta
item.description: People were killed and injured in a serious incident that resulted in a fire on one of Canada's busiest military bases in Alberta, Defense Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson
item.content:encoded: People were killed and injured in a serious incident that resulted in a fire on one of Canada's busiest military bases in Alberta, Defense Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday. "I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident" at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa. He did not say how many people were killed or injured, or what caused the "tragic" situation at the base in the east-central part of the province, about 210 km (130 miles) east of Edmonton. A major fire was still burning on Saturday evening, he said, adding: "I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory." The Canadian military and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating the incident, McGuinty said. Prime Minister Mark Carney posted on social media that the national government was "working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities." CFB Wainwright had 1,310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The town of Wainwright, population about 6,600, is just north of the base. The municipality posted on social media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district but no evacuation orders had been issued. General Jennie Carignan, the chief of Canada's Defense Staff, said on social media that the Canadian forces are fully engaged with federal, provincial and local authorities. "Our priority remains the welfare of our members, their families and their community," she said. (This story has been corrected to add the dropped word 'not' in paragraph 3.)

item.title: US wants Israel to 'crack down' on settler violence in West Bank, Rubio says
item.description: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Marco Rubio said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The United States wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers in the West Bank, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday. "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Rubio said. "We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff." His comments to reporters came after the widespread dissemination of video showing multiple individuals attacking Heidi Levine, an American photojournalist with the Washington Post. Levine was one of at least two people injured in the Friday incident, which took place as Israeli settlers [USN:L6N46304S TEXT:"attacked"] Palestinian civilians. European diplomats and a French mayor also were attacked in the occupied West Bank, Belgium's foreign minister said. The US State Department, Rubio said, has inquired about the event that included Levine's attack. Rubio, who spoke to reporters before boarding a flight to Uzbekistan, said he expects to hear back from the US Embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday. Israeli settlers in the West Bank have been involved in at least 170 attacks on Palestinians since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group.

item.title: What redistricting means for Tennessee voters
item.description: Redrawing the lines splits neighbors and groups them with people far away.
item.dc:creator: Ally J. Levine, Bianca Flowers, David Hood-Nuño
item.content:encoded: It’s a political fault line that leaves neighbors on both sides with less say. 9th District5th District The street outside Tammy Jo O'Neal's home has become a political boundary with big implications. The city of Memphis used to sit almost entirely in one congressional district. The new map splits O'Neal from neighbors across the street, each now belonging to districts with voters halfway across the state who have different needs and interests. O'Neal sees the new map as more than a split block. “There's this divide that's happening in our lives,not just in our districts.” District 5 District 9 Tammy Jo O’Neal sits for a portrait on the front porch of their home on Elzey Ave in Memphis, Tennessee, US, July 29, 2026. REUTERS/Seth Herald A citydivided By Bianca Flowers , David Hood-Nuño and Ally J. Levine Published Oct. 17, 2026 6:00 a.m. EDT What happens when congressional district lines are redrawn, splitting neighbors and grouping them with people far away Four years before the Memphis redistricting, Republicans used a similar strategy in drawing new maps for Nashville. They split the city, which had voted overwhelmingly Democratic for roughly 70 years, into three broader districts where Republicans can now easily prevail. Battles over redistricting have long been intertwined with racism and political power, particularly in southern states like Tennessee. Sixty-four years ago, a federal court found Tennessee diluted voting power in urban areas where majority Black voters lived and ordered the legislature to redraw its congressional districts. For decades, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was a powerful tool for Black voters, particularly in the South, to challenge discrimination and protect political power among people of color to elect representatives who would advocate for their communities. The act significantly increased Black and Hispanic representation in Congress by curtailing certain redistricting practices, including splitting people of color among many districts or concentrating them in some districts to limit their impact in others. But those protections have been steadily weakened. In 2013, when Democrat Barack Obama was president, the Supreme Court’s decision on the Alabama case Shelby County v. Holder gutted a provision requiring federal approval before states change voting laws or political maps. In April, the court narrowed the Voting Rights Act further in Louisiana v. Callais , making it harder to challenge new maps that dilute the voting power of communities of color. The court essentially required such challenges to prove that districts were drawn intentionally to discriminate on the basis of race, and not for other reasons. Republicans argue their redistricting in Tennessee and elsewhere is about party politics, not race. They point out that Democrats regularly redraw districts in states they control to give their party easier election wins. Democrats have done the same in California, for example, said Steve Hickey, chair of the Republican Party in Williamson County, a popular suburban area south of Nashville. “This is part of a bigger game being played nationally, and I don’t think it’s fair to say that this was done to gut” the Voting Rights Act, he said. Redistricting in the United States is generally controlled by state legislatures, which adjust voter maps after the once-a-decade census. Both parties have historically used the process to help their candidates win future elections. In 2025, at the urging of President Donald Trump, Texas launched an unusual mid-decade redistricting drive as part of a broader Republican push to gain congressional seats in half a dozen states, including Tennessee. Democrats responded with their own partisan redistricting in California and attempts that faltered in other states. Civil rights activists say Tennessee’s congressional districts, all of which currently favor Republicans, are now a testing ground for dismantling voting rights protections across the United States. “This lack of competition spills over and has racial implications,” said John Geer, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University who conducts polling in Tennessee. Reuters sought to quantify the impact of redistricting on the voters of Tennessee, examining public funding, demographics and socioeconomic factors to show why it’s important to residents when a city is split up like this. MemphisDistrict 9Suburbs of NashvilleDistrict 5District 8District 9 Population by race, one dot per person Black residents White residents Other races and ethnicities Memphis has the largest Black population in Tennessee. The city of some 630,000 people is 63% Black. Memphis accounted for 78% of the former District 9’s population, making it the only majority-Black district in the state. Earlier this year, the Tennessee legislature drew new district lines, splitting Memphis and its Black communities into three separate districts. The pieces of the city are now grouped with rural and suburban Tennesseans in districts that reach halfway across the state. Note: “White” and “Black” are non-Hispanic. “Other races and ethnicities” combines Hispanic or Latino residents of any race with the non-Hispanic categories Asian alone, American Indian and Alaska Native alone, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone, Some Other Race alone, and Two or More Races. Sources: US Census Bureau (2020 census redistricting data; TIGER/Line boundaries); Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 districts); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 districts); State of Tennessee and the City of Memphis Engineering Division (city limits); Tennessee Department of Transportation (roads) Reuters spoke to more than 35 redistricting scholars, political analysts, civic leaders, political candidates and voters about the consequences of redistricting for the most vulnerable communities in Tennessee’s two biggest cities. Cities faced the biggest impact because rural areas were already represented by a Republican and continue to be so after the redistricting, albeit in districts with different demographics. Before redistricting, both Nashville and Memphis were overwhelmingly Democratic districts in an otherwise Republican state. In 2024, District 9, including most of Memphis, went 71% for Democrat Steve Cohen. In 2020, Jim Cooper, a Democrat, ran unopposed in Nashville’s District 5, winning more than 99% of votes cast. In 2022, the new District 5 flipped, with the Republican candidate winning 57%. Tennessee’s new maps have combined city, suburban and rural populations that have widely varying needs and political preferences. The residents of Nashville and Memphis, for instance, are far more likely to struggle with poverty, housing, public safety and related issues. Residents there could now struggle to elect Congress members who prioritize policies to address these issues, according to Odessa Kelly, executive director of Stand Up Nashville, a nonprofit community organization that advocates for racial and economic equality. She said Black voters in Nashville no longer felt they had someone to stand up for them in Congress, from federal funding going to the city to critical votes on bills that directly affect city residents. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention developed the Social Vulnerability Index to gauge how well a community can withstand and recover from an emergency, and to identify which communities may need the most support. Shelby County, home to Memphis, ranks among the most vulnerable of Tennessee’s 95 counties on various indicators such as housing cost burden and lack of access to a vehicle. Memphis, Nashville residents rank higher in social vulnerability A US government index compares Tennessee communities on socioeconomic and demographic factors gauging their resilience to unexpected hardships. 25th 50th 75th 100th percentile Lower vulnerability Higher vulnerability Shelby County (Memphis) Minority status Racial or ethnic minority 100 Davidson County (Nashville) Housing and transportation In structures of 10+ units 97 No vehicle available 94 More people than rooms 60 Lives in group quarters 56 Mobile homes 0 Household characteristics Aged 17 and under 97 Single-parent household 96 Speaks English less than well 91 With a disability 9 Aged 65 and over 5 Socioeconomic status Housing cost burdened 100 Unemployed 86 No health insurance 76 Below 150% of poverty 50 No high school diploma (25+) 16 0 Chart showing where Shelby County and Davidson County rank among Tennessee’s 95 counties on 16 measures of the CDC’s Social Vulnerability Index, grouped into four themes, on a scale from the 0 to the 100th percentile with the other 93 counties as faint ticks. Both rank high on most measures — Shelby at the 100th percentile for racial or ethnic minority share and housing cost burden, Davidson at the 100th for apartments in large buildings and for people who speak English less than well. Both drop to the middle or bottom on poverty, the 50th percentile for Shelby and the 23rd for Davidson, and on residents aged 65 and over. Source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry Social Vulnerability Index 2022 In 2024, just over a third of Tennessee voters picked Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, and in 2020, Democrats won two congressional seats out of the state’s nine, carrying Nashville and Memphis. Now, every congressional district in Tennessee is considered “safe” for Republicans. Sandi Wells, a self-described “very conservative” voter from Williamson County, just outside Nashville, said it was “kind of odd” to group Memphis in the same district with parts of Williamson County 200 miles away. But she rejected the notion that districts should be drawn to protect Black voting power. “I don’t think we should have districts that are based on race,” she said. “I mean, that’s just ridiculous for anyone to even think that we should have that.” Shane Tinnin, a 52-year-old small business owner who maintains homes in both cities and has voted mostly for Democrats, understands that parties seek political power through redistricting but called the Memphis maps a particularly striking setback for Black political power. “In Nashville, it seemed really more like this is a political move,” he said, noting that it was not a Black-majority city. “When you do it in Memphis, where it’s an even more liberal district, but also a predominantly Black district, it just feels especially egregious to me.” Odessa Kelly, executive director at Stand Up Nashville, points to topics of focus for her and her team at a meeting in July. REUTERS/Seth Herald Volunteers for The Equity Alliance canvass through neighborhoods in Memphis to do “accountability” door knocks to speak with residents about elected officials following the GOP-led effort to redistrict the city. REUTERS/Seth Herald Securing funding Reuters examined how Nashville’s redistricting has impacted community project funding, under which lawmakers can seek federal money for local projects. Previously known as earmarks, community project funds returned to Congress with a more transparent process in fiscal year 2022 after a decade-long moratorium. A Reuters analysis found a dramatic shift in funding for Nashville after the city was split among three districts. Jim Cooper, a Democrat, steered most of the old 5th District’s project funding to Nashville in fiscal years 2022 and 2023. In the years since, only a small share of funding has gone toward projects in the city, including fiscal year 2027 requests still pending before Congress. Funding can vary greatly between representatives. Only John Rose, who currently represents the 6th District, has requested funding among the three members whose districts included Nashville after redistricting. Matt Van Epps and Andy Ogles have not pursued community project funding for their districts at all, arguing against such spending on principle. All three did not provide a comment or did not respond to a request to comment. Total Community Project Funding for districts that include Nashville After FY2023 FY2024 $18 mln $21 mln $2.5 mln Not Nashville $18 mln Nashville Nashville $3 mln $15.5 mln Before Two flow diagrams comparing Community Project Funds before and after redistricting. In the year before, when Nashville sat in a single district, District 5 received $18 million and $15.5 million of it went to Nashville, with $2.5 million going elsewhere. In the year after, with Nashville divided across three districts, Districts 5, 6 and 7 received $21 million between them but only $3 million reached Nashville, while $18 million went to areas outside the city. Note: Data show the total funding for districts that include Nashville. Before the 2022 redistricting, Nashville was contained in District 5. After, it was split between Districts 5, 6 and 7. Source: US Government Accountability Office The shift away from community funding jeopardized future funding for projects like public housing, healthcare centers, buildings for the two historically Black colleges in the city and public transportation in Nashville. For Memphis, a similar decline in earmark funding would be a big loss. Since 2022, District 9 Representative Steve Cohen, a Democrat, pulled in $52.6 million for projects based in Memphis, according to figures published by the US Government Accountability Office and the US House Committee on Appropriations. That’s 83% of all the community project funding for District 9 in that period. District 7 State capitol District 6 State House of Representatives The Tennessee State Capitol building and Legislative Plaza, which is undergoing construction. REUTERS/Seth Herald Another important role for a member of Congress is to act as a middleman between people in their district and the government, helping negotiate the bureaucracy of Washington. When Cooper represented Nashville, he fielded calls about immigration paperwork, passports, Medicare, Social Security checks and more, said Tennessee State Senator Charlane Oliver, who worked as a community liaison and communications staffer in Cooper’s congressional office from 2017 to 2019. “He would show up to the cookout, the fish fry, the parades, the meetings and the galas,” she said. That kind of interaction is harder if the representative does not have a local office. When Nashville was split, only one representative, Mark Green of District 7, kept an office near the center of the city. That office was closed when Van Epps took over the seat in 2025, leaving no offices within the city limits. Constituents in Nashville have to drive 36 miles on average to visit a congressional district office, a Reuters analysis found, compared with less than 10 miles when Cooper represented Nashville, the seat of Davidson County. Average trip to Congressional district office District 5 +39 miles after District 6 +17 mi District 7 +16 mi 0 10 20 30 40 50 miles 9 miles before redistricting A chart of the average driving distance for Nashville residents to their closest congressional district office, shown for each of the three districts the city is now split among. A dark bar common to all three marks the 9-mile average from when Nashville sat in a single district, flagged on the scale as “9 miles before redistricting.” A lighter bar extends past it to each district’s new average: District 5 adds 39 miles, reaching about 47; District 6 adds 17, reaching about 25; and District 7 adds 16, reaching about 24 miles. Note: Data shows the average driving distance for Nashville residents in each district to their closest district office. District 7’s offices are those open under Rep. Matt Van Epps, who won the seat after Mark Green resigned in 2025. Green kept an office in downtown Nashville; which put District 7’s average at 5 miles. That office no longer exists. Source: Reuters analysis of congressional district office locations Van Epps and the other two Republicans running this year in Nashville districts, Johnny Garrett and Charlie Hatcher, did not respond to Reuters requests for interviews for this story. Most city buses don’t operate far enough outside the city to visit a congressional district office in Cookeville, more than an hour’s drive away. Kyle Cook, who works in the public library, said Cooper’s office used to be just upstairs from his own in downtown Nashville. “Now, if I wanted to advocate just as a regular citizen for better busing, I would have to call this office in Cookeville and it’s just not the same kind of relationship,” Cook said. Who speaks for Memphis? Cohen represented Memphis for 19 years but stood down when new maps were passed, saying “these districts were drawn to beat me.” State Representative Justin Pearson, a progressive Democrat, is campaigning to represent the 9th District. Pearson gained national attention in 2023 when he was temporarily expelled from the Tennessee House, for what Republicans described as a breach of decorum when he joined a protest on gun control . Polls show him trailing Brent Taylor, a Republican state senator endorsed by President Donald Trump. But Pearson said Tennessee was “not a lost cause” for Democrats. In an interview with Reuters, Pearson described the Memphis redistricting as “one of the most significant political deprivations of Black political power and accessibility to the ballot since the end of Reconstruction in Tennessee.” Tennessee State Representative Justin Pearson stands for a portrait in the Cooper Young neighborhood in Memphis. REUTERS/Seth Herald Taylor has defended redistricting efforts in Tennessee as a “compliance measure” in response to the 2026 US Supreme Court ruling that he says prohibits the consideration of racial data when redrawing political boundaries. Asked about his top priorities in such a diverse district spanning downtown Memphis to rural Fayette County, Taylor pointed to inflation. “Everybody feels the pain right now,” he said. “When I filled up my car the other day, it was $112. People feel the pinch at the gas pump. They feel higher prices when they go to the grocery store. Everything we do costs more.” Civil Miller-Watkins, an eighth-grade math teacher in Fayette County who was drawn into District 9 and plans to vote for Pearson, said the needs of voters in her area differ from those in Memphis. Rural voters worry about access to broadband, ambulances, grocery stores and schools, she said. “All of these interests are very legitimate,” Miller-Watkins said. “But I don’t know if any community can say they’re going to have effective representation.” Pearson, the Democrat, says he’s campaigned in 15 counties that now come under the district and economic hardship is the common thread. “That’s hurting people who are working class in Memphis, just like it’s hurting farmers in Savannah, Tennessee,” he said. “We have a lot more in common.” Urban 96% Suburban 4% Shelby County 737,000 people live in an urban county in District 9 Tipton County 31,000 live in a suburban county District 9 After Urban 35% Suburban 27% Memphis Nashville Williamson 107k Shelby 269k people Rutherford 39k Maury 33k Memphis area Small towns 22% Bedford 50k Lincoln 35k McNairy 26k Giles 30k Hardeman 25k Marshall 34k Lawrence 44k Hardin 27k Wayne 16k Moore 7k Rural 16% Before redistricting Fayette 25k Two panels comparing the counties that make up Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District before and after the 2026 redraw, with each county drawn at an area proportional to its population. Before, the district is almost entirely one place: urban Shelby County, home to Memphis, fills the panel with roughly 737,000 people, beside a thin sliver for suburban Tipton County’s ~31,000. After, 767,872 people are spread across 15 counties in four groups. Urban counties make up 35% of the district; suburban counties comprise 27%, small towns 22% and rural counties 16%. Note: Counties are grouped by the National Center for Health Statistics urban–rural classification. “Large central metro” was renamed to “Urban”, “Large fringe metro” to “Suburban”, “Micropolitan” to “Small towns” and “Noncore” was renamed “Rural” in this graphic. Sources: US Census; NCHS Urban-Rural Classification Scheme; Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 district); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 district) Pearson said he was concerned that some voters were confused about which district they were in and that this could hurt turnout. Pearson’s advocacy for criminal justice reform and affordability has appealed to younger Democratic Party voters like 27-year-old Marko Jankov. But Jankov, who identifies as a Democratic Socialist, lives in a part of Memphis that was moved out of the 9th District and he said he was less motivated to vote for other Democrats when polls showed them unlikely to win. “They want to make it a psychological thing, where you think you can’t win,” Jankov said. The changes are exposing a rural-urban divide. Debby Gould, president of the non-partisan League of Women Voters of Tennessee, said voters of all backgrounds had concerns. “This is a time when we really have to strengthen urban-rural links and to come up with shared values,” she said. “Because rural voters are also feeling left out on this.” Hickey, the Williamson County Republican chair, said it was up to candidates to show they could work for all their constituents: “They’re going to have to put a lot of miles in their car.” Opening photo Elzey Avenue in Memphis, a dividing line between Congressional District 9 and Congressional District 5, following a Republican-led effort to redistrict Memphis. item.title: CoreWeave's CEO sold nearly $1 billion of stock since IPO, filings show
item.description: The sales began about two months after the stock hit a record high in June 2025.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: CoreWeave (CRWV.O) CEO Michael Intrator and entities linked to him have sold nearly $1 billion of stock, mostly under prearranged trading plans, since the AI cloud company's IPO in March last year, according to regulatory filings. The sales began about two months after the stock hit a record high in June 2025. The shares have tumbled since and were on track to lose about 24% this week [USN:L4N4620ZT TEXT:"as investors worried about"] the Nvidia-backed company's heavy capital spending and the debt needed to fund it amid rising bets on interest-rate hikes. CoreWeave did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Here are some more details: The sales totaled more than 10 million shares, according to the filings. As of Thursday's close, CoreWeave had a valuation of $38.44 billion. The sales were made by Intrator and affiliated entities such as Omnadora Capital, where Intrator serves as managing member, and two trusts. Most of these sales, excluding roughly $40 million, were made under prearranged trading plans that allow executives to sell shares on a preset schedule, and do not necessarily reflect management's view of the business. The roughly $40 million that was not part of prearranged plans was sell-to-cover sales, where shares were sold on the market to pay taxes on vested stock. The selling occurred as CoreWeave rapidly expanded its data-center footprint and increased spending on Nvidia chips to meet demand for AI computing, while building a revenue backlog of [USN:L6N4590TM TEXT:"more than $129 billion"]. In August, the company raised its annual capital expenditure forecast to be between [USN:L4N4481ER TEXT:"$35 billion and $39 billion"].

item.title: Wall St Week Ahead As AI rally wobbles, stock market's spotlight turns to earnings
item.description: Stumbles in the market-leading AI trade are set to test investor confidence in the rally in the coming week as Wall Street focuses on quarterly results due from key players including Meta Platforms .
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: Stumbles in the market-leading AI trade are set to test investor confidence in the rally in the coming week as Wall Street focuses on quarterly results due from key players including Meta Platforms (META.O) . AI-linked stocks, central to [USN:L6N45R12W TEXT:"the bull market"] that just marked its fourth anniversary, [USN:L6N460140 TEXT:"struggled in recent days"], with sharp declines in shares of semiconductor companies and tech hardware firms such as Dell Technologies (DELL.N) . Meta, among the hyperscalers spending massively to build AI data centers, highlights the upcoming week of quarterly reports, along with semiconductor firms Lam Research (LRCX.O) and Texas Instruments (TXN.O) and Elon Musk -led companies SpaceX (SPCX.O) and Tesla (TSLA.O) . "It certainly feels like the narrative in the market is a little bit jittery," said Garrett Melson, portfolio strategist with Natixis Investment Managers Solutions. "Clearly there's a lot of uncertainty around where AI stands right now." Worries rippled through markets over risks tied to [USN:L6N461185 TEXT:"the financing of the AI build-out boom"], which has lifted profits for a wide swath of companies and boosted economic growth. Investors were watching [USN:L4N461208 TEXT:"developments with CoreWeave"] (CRWV.O) , an AI cloud company with about $50 billion in debt. This week, its shares tumbled. In other recent signs of caution, strategists at Deutsche Bank and RBC Capital Markets separately pulled back on their recommendations of the tech sector. On October 9, Deutsche Bank strategists said the rotation into tech had "run far and the risk-reward no longer looks favorable in the near term." Dragged down by the swoon in heavyweight tech and AI stocks, the S&P 500 (.SPX) posted its biggest weekly drop since June. But the benchmark index was only about 2% below its record high set this month. Other sectors, which lagged as tech shined last month, posted solid gains on the week, including healthcare and consumer staples. "This is very much an on-off switch type of market," Melson said. "When AI is working, it sucks all the oxygen out of the room for the rest of the sectors." META KICKS OFF HYPERSCALER RESULTS US reporting season heats up next week, with investors counting on robust performance. S&P 500 companies are expected to have increased earnings by more than 30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES. Massive outlays on AI data centers and infrastructure underpin the profit jump. Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers that combined are expected to increase their capital spending to about $1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs. Investors are eager for signs the companies can show returns on the investments, which would build confidence that the spending is sustainable. "One of the most important takeaways of earnings season is whether or not the profitability of the hyperscalers can grow faster than the pace of their capex," said Kevin Shea, senior equity analyst at BNY Wealth. Shares of Meta, whose market capitalization was about $1.8 trillion, have risen in recent weeks as it launched its Muse AI assistant "With the cost of capital going up, this capex blowout is going to become more expensive, which raises the bar for returns," said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services. "Meta is going to be the first up to try to provide some color around that question." SEMIS, TESLA, NETFLIX ALSO ON TAP Chip companies have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the capital spending boom, but the stocks have cooled off. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index (.SOX) has slumped about 12% this month, although it remained up 57% on the year, compared with a roughly 12% year-to-date gain for the S&P 500. Wednesday's reports from Lam Research and Texas Instruments could offer broader indications of demand in the semiconductor industry. Lam Research shares are up 54% in 2026, while Texas Instruments stock is up 59%. Elsewhere, investors will focus on results from Musk-run companies with market values well over $1 trillion: SpaceX — the newly public space company that also has an AI business — and Tesla, another signature stock of the tech-driven bull market. Streaming company Netflix (NFLX.O) , consumer products company Procter & Gamble (PG.N) and engine maker GE Aerospace (GE.N) are among other high-profile reports in the coming week. The rise in Treasury yields and prospects for further rate hikes from the Federal Reserve also remain front-burner issues for stock investors. Hot inflation data this week boosted bets on another rate increase at the Fed's meeting at the end of October. Futures pricing suggested most investors still expect the US central bank to wait until its meeting in December to raise rates for a second time this year. "Another strong earnings season should help equities withstand moderately higher rates," analysts at UBS Global Wealth Management said in a note on Thursday.

item.title: Why CoreWeave's troubles are rattling the AI boom
item.description: CoreWeave's mounting debt is raising concerns about the AI boom, as investors question whether demand can justify the billions being borrowed to build data centers.
item.dc:creator: Anhata Rooprai, Aditya Soni
item.content:encoded: CoreWeave's (CRWV.O) mounting debt is raising fresh concerns about the AI boom, as investors question whether demand can justify the billions being borrowed to build data centres. Shares and bonds of the Nvidia-backed (NVDA.O) company [USN:L4N46112V TEXT:"have tumbled"] despite its CEO's assurances of a strong contract backlog, fueling a broader selloff in technology stocks. Here is why investors are worried and what its troubles could mean for the industry. WHAT DOES COREWEAVE DO? CoreWeave rents out computing power from Nvidia processors to companies developing and running AI, including Microsoft (MSFT.O) and OpenAI. It is one of the leading "neocloud" providers, a group of newer cloud companies that are growing rapidly to meet demand for scarce and expensive AI chips. These neocloud companies give customers access to computing power without requiring them to build their own data centers. However, supplying such capacity requires heavy upfront investment in chips and infrastructure, often financed with debt. WHAT IS ITS FINANCIAL SITUATION? The company, which has never turned a profit, has about $50 billion in debt, according to data compiled by LSEG. It raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion in August [USN:L4N4481ER TEXT:"to between $35 billion and $39 billion"]. Analysts expect revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion. The yields on its bonds due in 2031, which are rated junk, have spiked to about 16%, while the cost of insuring its debt against default has climbed to about 1,000 basis points, reflecting growing concern among creditors. CEO Mike Intrator told employees in an internal memo seen by Reuters that its deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations. The company had a $104.2 billion revenue backlog at the end of the second quarter, followed by [USN:L6N4590TM TEXT:"more than $25 billion"] in new commitments early in the third quarter. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also downplayed the concerns, saying CoreWeave's financial strength is improving and he sees no need to backstop it. The chip giant has agreed to buy unsold CoreWeave capacity through April 2032. WHY IT COULD BE A CANARY IN THE COAL MINE CoreWeave's business depends on two things: demand for AI computing and lenders' willingness to finance the infrastructure supplying it. But a selloff in its shares suggests a lack of confidence among investors in the latter, even as the company cites strong demand. The concern is not that AI demand will collapse, but that higher borrowing costs could make the business harder to sustain if demand were to weaken sharply. "It looks more like investors questioning how the build-out is being funded than a sudden collapse in appetite for AI computing," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. "CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade's canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. WHY ARE MARKETS FRETTING? Investors are questioning whether AI revenue can grow fast enough to cover the cost of building and financing the infrastructure. CoreWeave has to spend heavily upfront before it can collect the revenue from its contracts. Higher interest rates could drive up financing costs and further squeeze returns. The hardware itself poses another risk. Chips lose value as newer generations arrive, pushing providers to spend even more to replace them. The concerns, however, go beyond CoreWeave. US technology giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure this year. THE DOWNSIDE SCENARIO One potential consequence would be a broader financing squeeze, with lenders demanding higher returns or becoming less willing to fund other AI projects. That could force providers to scale back expansion, curbing equipment purchases and affecting the computing capacity customers expect. A setback could also deepen doubts that the AI investment frenzy is outpacing returns, piling further pressure on technology stocks. The impact of the fallout would depend on how the business is reorganized, and CoreWeave's ties to major technology companies do not, by themselves, mean its failure would trigger a wider financial crisis. WHO ELSE BEARS THE RISK? Gartner estimates about 80% of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, warning that expected AI revenue will not support profitable returns on all planned infrastructure spending. Neocloud rivals Nebius (NBIS.O) , Applied Digital (APLD.O) and Iren (IREN.O) have fallen in the recent selloff. The cost of default protection has risen for SoftBank (9984.T) , which is betting heavily on OpenAI. Meanwhile, spreads for Amazon (AMZN.O) , Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Meta (META.O) and Nvidia have also reached records, although they have risen much more slowly than CoreWeave's. However, these companies also have larger cash flows and stronger balance sheets.

item.title: Skateboarding-On the road again: Spain's Poncelet sets world speed record
item.description: The downhill skateboarder reached more than 94 miles per hour. "If a record has stood for nine years, you don't just break it by a little bit, you destroy it."
item.dc:creator: Ruairidh Barlow
item.content:encoded: Spanish downhill skateboarder Diego Poncelet did not just want to set a standing world speed record; he wanted to know what it felt like going 150 kph with no brakes. The two-time world champion finally achieved that goal on September 22 in Canada when he reached a speed of 151.83 kph, nine years after Pete Connolly clocked 146.73 kph on the very same road. "If a record has stood for nine years, you don't just break it by a little bit, you destroy it," Poncelet told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday. "If I'm honest with myself, my real objective was 150 kph. That was the dream." The Red Bull athlete began work on the attempt four years ago, but his search for a road with the required gradient to spur him to record speeds came to nothing. Finally, Poncelet had to accept that Route 362 in Les Eboulements, two hours north-east of Quebec City, is a "miracle". "A lot of people told me it wasn't possible anymore because of large cracks and potholes," the 27-year-old said. "There was a real question over whether the road had deteriorated too much." On a specially designed 14 kg skateboard, in shoes soled with car tyre rubber, Poncelet launched himself into the abyss. "That road in particular was terrifying because you're doing about 110 kph and suddenly the road disappears, you can't see it. All you can see is the St. Lawrence River," said Poncelet. Usually when Poncelet plunges downhill, he has two plastic slide pucks attached to gloves he uses to slow himself. Not this time. "It was very difficult mentally, because of how steep it is and because of the equipment I was using, I couldn't brake. Once you start the run, whatever happens, you have to get to the bottom at full speed," he said. "You can't brake because at those speeds you would go flying." Poncelet, who has a degree in international relations, says it is almost as if he enters a Zen-like state when travelling at such frightening speeds. "I like to say it's as if there's a wise person inside your mind and you let that person take control," he added. "That wise person is your subconscious. It's an incredible feeling, everything feels perfect. "It's like high-consequence meditation," Poncelet grins.

item.title: AI credit worries send default insurance to record high
item.description: Investors rushed to hedge against the risk of credit stress building in the AI trade.
item.dc:creator: Tom Westbrook, Amanda Cooper
item.content:encoded: The cost of insuring against tech defaults struck record highs on Thursday, as investors rushed to hedge against the risk of credit stress building in the AI trade, with heavily indebted data centre operators like CoreWeave (CRWV.O) hit hardest. Hotter-than-expected [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"US inflation data"], together with mounting expectations for higher interest rates, are adding to concerns about how quickly massive investment in artificial intelligence will translate into profits, as well as whether heavily indebted companies can generate returns fast enough to service mounting interest costs. Credit default swaps (CDS) are sending a warning signal to markets. The standouts were five-year CDS spreads for CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , which blew past 1,100 bps, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data , while the yield on the company's 2031 bond rose to as much as 16% before retreating to around 14%. Cloud computing giant Oracle (ORCL.N) , which has also stirred up investor angst because of its vast borrowing, saw its CDS near 300 bps, bringing the rise this week to around 31 bps. CDS for Nvidia (NVDA.O) , Franco-Italian chipmaker STMicroelectronics and SpaceX (SPCX.O) , which offers some AI services, rose sharply. CoreWeave, a loss-making "neocloud" company that owes nearly $50 billion, according to LSEG data, is in the eye of the storm. "CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade’s canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. "Its bonds have sold off sharply ... this is a sign that investors might be going off the AI investment narrative, which has included massive debt issuance to fund AI ambitions." A surge in quarterly revenue from [USN:L6N4601AA TEXT:"AI developer Anthropic"] did little to calm the market's nerves. According to an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting with the company's leadership in San Francisco on Wednesday, third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter. Anthropic is targeting a valuation of $2 trillion. DEBT MARKET JITTERS CDS spreads show the number of basis points charged for default protection. The greater the perceived risk of a credit event, the wider the spread, meaning the 1,000 bps for CoreWeave CDS implies a risk of default in the coming five years of 64%, up from around 30% a year ago. Earlier this week, [USN:L1N45Z07U TEXT:"Broadcom Chief Executive"] Hock Tan compared the investor rush for anything AI-related to "casino gambling." CoreWeave stock was down another 2% on Thursday, following a 15% slide on Wednesday, meaning nearly a fifth of the company's value has burned up in two days. CoreWeave shares have now fallen 10% since the start of this year, while those of rival Nebius (NBIS.O) , for which there are no publicly tradable CDS, are up about 114%. Credit default swap spreads for Amazon (AMZN.O) , Alphabet (GOOGL.O) and Meta (META.O) also traded at record highs, data from LSEG and S&P Global Market Intelligence showed, though they have risen far more slowly than Oracle, or CoreWeave. "This is not the first time we’ve had a sizeable market wobble on the back of AI fears, but as we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action. AI financing costs aren’t dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges," Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid said.

item.content:encoded: Trump dispose d'un délai pour se prononcer sur les sanctions contre la Russie, dit Rubio 17 octobre (Reuters) - Le secrétaire d'Etat américain Marco Rubio a déclaré samedi que Donald Trump disposait d'un délai pouvant aller jusqu'à 60 jours pour évaluer l'impact économique des sanctions et des droits de douane liés à la Russie. L'Egypte prête à contribuer à la sécurité de l'Arabie saoudite 18 octobre (Reuters) - L'Egypte est prête à apporter à l'Arabie saoudite le soutien nécessaire à la défense de sa sécurité et de sa stabilité face aux attaques des Houthis, a déclaré dimanche la présidence égyptienne. Première apparition publique du pape depuis son opération pour un cancer du poumon CITE DU VATICAN, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Le pape Léon XIV a promis dimanche de reprendre progressivement ses fonctions à la tête de l'Eglise catholique lors de sa première apparition publique depuis son opération subie il y a cinq jours pour un cancer du poumon. Les USA ont repris le partage de renseignements avec l'Ukraine, dit Zelensky 18 octobre (Reuters) - Les États-Unis ont repris le partage de renseignements avec l'Ukraine pour l'aider à se défendre contre les attaques de missiles russes, a déclaré dimanche le président Volodimir Zelensky. Trump apporte son soutien à Netanyahu pour les élections en Israël WASHINGTON, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump a apporté dimanche son soutien à Benjamin Netanyahu en vue des prochaines élections législatives israéliennes. Un ministre russe au FMI boycotté par les Européens Plusieurs délégués du comité de pilotage du Fonds monétaire international (FMI) ont quitté samedi une réunion au moment où le ministre russe des Finances, Anton Silouanov, prenait la parole, rapportent trois sources présentes. Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital samedi après-midi pour regagner le Vatican, quatre jours après avoir subi une intervention chirurgicale pour un cancer du poumon. Zelensky dénonce de nouvelles restrictions imposées par Starlink L'Ukraine n'est pas en mesure d'utiliser ses systèmes d'interception contre les attaques de drones russes en raison de restrictions de vitesse imposées par Starlink, a déclaré samedi le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky, ajoutant que Kyiv discutait de cette question avec des responsables américains. Des Palestiniens et des responsables européens attaqués par des colons en Cisjordanie occupée TAYBEH, Cisjordanie, 17 octobre (Reuters) - Des colons juifs masqués ont attaqué des Palestiniens, des représentants de l'Eglise catholique et des responsables européens en Cisjordanie occupée, a annoncé samedi le ministre belge des Affaires étrangères.

item.content:encoded: France-Macron dénonce la violence débridée et promet des aides PARIS, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Le président Emmanuel Macron a dénoncé dimanche la "violence débridée de factieux de la mouvance d'ultra-gauche et de délinquants", tout en appelant les Français en général et les partis politiques en particulier au dialogue et au sens de la responsabilité. 855 interpellations samedi à Paris, décès d'un manifestant d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire - préfecture PARIS, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Un manifestant est décédé à la suite d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire samedi à Paris lors des manifestations contre la vie chère, pendant lesquelles 855 interpellations ont été effectuées, ce qui représente un "chiffre record", a déclaré dimanche la préfecture de police. Paris condamne l'agression d'un maire français par des colons juifs PARIS, 18 octobre (Reuters) - La France a condamné dimanche l'agression "gravissime" par des colons juifs du maire d'Aulnoye-Aymeries survenue la veille dans le village palestinien de Taybeh. France et Allemagne d'accord sur un plan pour l'automobile La France et l'Allemagne ont annoncé vendredi un accord sur une "approche commune" visant à garantir l'avenir de l'industrie automobile européenne, avec un accent mis à la fois sur la transition énergétique et sur une production des véhicules en Europe. Les tortues caouannes, sentinelles du réchauffement en Méditerranée Sous un ciel baigné de lune, des bébés tortues sortent du sable sur la côte méditerranéenne turque et se hâtent vers la mer, dans un cycle naturel ancestral de plus en plus menacé par le changement climatique. Une étoile verte récemment découverte émerveille les astronomes Pour la première fois, des astronomes ont identifié une étoile verte, un vestige stellaire dense appelé "naine blanche", qui a pris une teinte fantomatique de vert chartreuse après avoir absorbé des débris rocheux provenant de planètes qui, autrefois, gravitaient autour d’elle. La santé du pape Léon en "amélioration constante", dit le Vatican Le pape Léon XIV continue de se remettre de son intervention chirurgicale subie mardi pour un nodule cancéreux au poumon, a déclaré vendredi le Vatican, soulignant "l'amélioration constante" de son état de santé. Le pape Léon XIV se rétablit comme prévu de son opération d'un cancer du poumon Le rétablissement du pape Léon XIV de son opération d'un cancer du poumon suit son cours, a annoncé jeudi le Vatican, qui précise que le souverain pontife de 71 ans a recommencé à travailler. Les dirigeants de l'UE se réunissent en sommet, tensions en vue sur le budget Les chefs d'Etat et de gouvernement de l'Union européenne se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour un sommet lors duquel devraient être mises en exergue les divergences sur l'ampleur du prochain budget pluriannuel et sur les priorités de dépense du bloc communautaire, sans accord attendu dans l'immédiat. Macron va effectuer une tournée dans le Golfe, sécurité et énergie au menu Emmanuel Macron effectuera en début de semaine prochaine une tournée dans le Golfe afin de "poursuivre sa mobilisation" auprès de dirigeants régionaux pour revenir à la stabilité et à la libre circulation dans le détroit d'Ormuz, voie cruciale pour les livraisons énergétiques mondiales, a dit mercredi l'Elysée.
